title: Historic Upset: Democrat Scott Colom Flips Mississippi Senate Seat
snippet: In a stunning midterm upset, Democrat Scott Colom narrowly ousted Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, becoming Mississippi's first Black U.S. Senator in over 140 years.
content:
JACKSON, Miss. — In one of the most stunning political upsets in recent history, Democrat Scott Colom has narrowly defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, expanding the Democratic Senate majority and flipping a seat in one of the nation's most reliably red states.

According to final tallies from the Associated Press, Colom secured 49.2% of the vote compared to Hyde-Smith’s 48.7% in a hard-fought contest that took more than a week after Election Day to call. The victory brings the Democratic Senate caucus to 55 seats following a sweeping midterm election cycle.

A Breakthrough Historic Victory

Colom’s victory marks a significant milestone in Southern politics. The 43-year-old former prosecutor becomes the first elected Black U.S. senator from Mississippi since the Reconstruction era more than 140 years ago. He is also the first Democrat to represent the Magnolia State in the U.S. Senate since 1989.

A native of Columbus, Mississippi, Colom earned his law degree from the University of Wisconsin before rising through the state's legal ranks. In 2015, he made state history by becoming the first Black district attorney elected to represent a majority-white voting district in Mississippi.

President Joe Biden nominated Colom for a federal judgeship on the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi in 2022, a nomination initially endorsed by key Mississippi Republicans, including former Gov. Phil Bryant. However, Hyde-Smith blocked the appointment in the Senate, citing political disagreements over campaign funding and public statements on transgender issues.

Capitalizing on a Stumble

Mississippi was not expected to be competitive this cycle, but vulnerabilities began showing in Hyde-Smith's campaign early on. While Republican Sen. Roger Wicker won reelection comfortably in 2024, Hyde-Smith faced growing public frustration over cost-of-living concerns and inflation.

The race flipped in mid-October after Colom released a viral campaign ad targeting Hyde-Smith's response to rising grocery prices. When questioned about high beef costs during a local television interview, Hyde-Smith remarked that "all commodities go through peaks and valleys" and noted that consumers have "so many proteins to choose from."

Colom's ad featured everyday Mississippians mocking the "proteins" comment, quickly generating nearly 19 million views online and prompting national Democratic organizations to pour millions of dollars into the state during the closing weeks of the campaign. High-profile Democrats, including former Presidents Barack Obama and Bill Clinton, campaigned or voiced support for Colom in the final stretch.

Looking Ahead

Hyde-Smith formally conceded the race in a video message posted to X on Wednesday evening. "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said, offering her congratulations to Colom.

Speaking to reporters as late ballots were counted, Colom emphasized his focus on working-class economic issues, including lowering everyday prices for voters across the political spectrum. His victory leaves Alaska as the sole remaining uncalled U.S. Senate contest from the midterm elections.
